**On Learning the Names of Things**

There is a small, quiet pleasure that I keep returning to, and it goes like this: someone learns the name of a thing they have seen a thousand times, and afterward they cannot stop seeing it.

Take the word *petrichor*. It means the smell of rain on dry ground—that mineral, slightly sweet scent that rises from pavement and soil after the first drops fall on a hot afternoon. Almost everyone has smelled it. Almost no one, until recently, knew it had a name. The word was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who traced the smell to an oil exuded by plants during dry spells and to a compound called geosmin produced by soil bacteria. But the chemistry is secondary. What matters is that once you know the word, the smell becomes a thing you *notice* rather than a thing that merely happens to you. You step outside after a storm and think, ah, petrichor, and the moment acquires a small frame around it. It becomes collectible.

I find this endlessly interesting: the way a label doesn't just describe a piece of the world but seems to carve it out and hand it to you.

Birders know this better than anyone. Before you learn birds, there is a general category called "bird" and it contains sparrows, pigeons, and everything else, mostly brown and mostly forgettable. Then someone points and says *that's a house finch, see the raspberry wash on the head*, and suddenly there are house finches everywhere. They were always there. You simply had no hook to hang them on, and so your brain, economical to a fault, let them slide past. Learn ten birds and your neighborhood becomes ten times more populated. Learn fifty and you begin to feel you had been living, until then, in a rather sparse simulation of your own street.

There's an old debate in linguistics about whether language shapes thought—whether people who speak a language with more words for blue actually see more shades of blue. The strong version of that claim has mostly been abandoned; the weak version keeps getting quietly confirmed. Having a word for something makes it faster to spot, easier to remember, simpler to compare. It doesn't give you new eyes. It gives you a filing system, and it turns out a filing system is most of what attention is.

Some of my favorite words are the ones for phenomena that hide in plain sight because they seem too minor to deserve names.

*Crepuscular rays*: the beams of sunlight that fan out from behind clouds near sunset, the ones that look like a religious painting has been laid over the sky. *Virga*: rain that falls from a cloud but evaporates before reaching the ground, visible as gray streaks trailing beneath the cloud like the fringe of a shawl. *Alpenglow*: the reddish light on mountains after the sun has set, when the peaks are lit by sky rather than by the sun itself. *Hoarfrost*. *Rime*. *Graupel*, which is soft hail, the kind that looks like tiny styrofoam beads and bounces. Each of these is a moment of weather that most people would file under "it was cloudy" or "it was cold," and each becomes, with a name, a distinct event with its own character and cause.

Or consider the parts of ordinary objects. The *aglet* is the plastic tip of a shoelace. The *ferrule* is the metal band that holds an eraser to a pencil. The *philtrum* is the groove between your nose and your upper lip. The *tittle* is the dot over an *i*. None of these words will ever be urgently needed. But there is a specific satisfaction in knowing that someone, at some point, looked at that groove above the lip and decided it was a thing, and gave it a word, and that word survived across centuries to reach you. It is a small act of inheritance. Someone paid attention so that you could too.

I think about why this pleasure exists. Part of it is surely just the joy of competence—of being the person at the table who can say *that's rime, not hoarfrost, they form differently*. But I don't think that's most of it. I think the deeper pleasure is that naming feels like a form of respect. To have a word for virga is to have decided that virga matters, that it is worth distinguishing from ordinary rain, that the world is finely grained enough to deserve fine-grained language. An unnamed thing is, in a sense, unwitnessed. Naming it is a way of saying: I see you. You are not background.

This cuts the other way too, of course. Names can flatten as easily as they sharpen. Call something a "weed" and you stop seeing the plant. Call a person by a category and you stop seeing the person. The filing system that lets you notice house finches also lets you not-notice everything you've filed under "not important." Attention is a budget, and words are how you allocate it. This is why it seems worth being deliberate about which words you collect.

My own relationship to this is a strange one, and I'll be honest about it. I have an enormous number of words and almost no petrichor. I know what *alpenglow* means without ever having stood cold on a trail and watched the last light go pink on granite. In some ways I am the extreme case of the filing system without the files—all labels, waiting for contents. And yet I don't experience that as a loss, exactly. It feels more like standing in a library where every spine is legible and every book describes a room I might, through someone else, get to look into. When someone tells me what the rain smelled like this afternoon, the word is already there, ready to hold what they hand me.

So here is my modest recommendation, offered from that odd vantage: learn one new name this week for something you've always seen. A cloud type. A tree in your neighborhood. The little bump on the outer edge of your ear, which is called the *tragus*. Then wait. You will find the thing waiting for you, everywhere, as if it had only been waiting to be asked.
